title: Why Did Rebekah Cover Jacob’s Hands With Goat Skins?
paragraphs: Why Did Rebekah Cover Jacob’s Hands With Goat Skins?

The disturbing detail in Genesis 27 wasn’t random. Jacob was about to walk into his blind father’s tent wearing his brother’s clothes, carrying his brother’s smell, and hiding beneath the skin of something that had just died—and what happened next exposes something painfully familiar about the human heart.
There is a moment in Genesis that becomes more unsettling the longer you sit with it.
An old father can barely see.
A mother is moving quickly.
A younger son is wearing clothes that do not belong to him.
Food is being prepared to imitate another son’s cooking.
And then Rebekah does something strangely specific.
She takes the skins of young goats and puts them on Jacob’s hands and around the smooth part of his neck.
The Hebrew of Genesis 27:16 reads:
“וְאֵת עֹרֹת גְּדָיֵי הָעִזִּים הִלְבִּישָׁה עַל־יָדָיו וְעַל חֶלְקַת צַוָּארָיו”
Ve’et ‘orot gedaye ha‘izzim hilbishah ‘al-yadav ve‘al chelqat tzavvarav.
In straightforward English:
“And the skins of the young goats she put on his hands and on the smooth part of his neck.”
That wording matters.

The Hebrew ‘orot means “skins” or “hides.” Gedaye refers to young goats or kids. Hilbishah comes from a verb associated with clothing or putting something on. And chelqat describes the smooth part of Jacob’s neck.
Rebekah was, quite literally, clothing Jacob’s smoothness with another creature’s skin.
Why?
Because Jacob had a problem.
He was trying to receive something while pretending to be someone he was not.
And his father knew the difference between the two sons.
Earlier, Genesis describes Esau as unusually hairy. Jacob himself understands the danger immediately when Rebekah proposes the deception:
“Behold, Esau my brother is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man.” — Genesis 27:11
Jacob knows Isaac may touch him.
And if Isaac touches him, the lie may collapse.
Notice something uncomfortable about Jacob’s objection.
His first recorded concern is not simply, “Mother, this would be wrong.”
His concern is that he might get caught.
He tells Rebekah that if his father feels him, he may appear to be a deceiver and bring a curse upon himself instead of a blessing.
That is frighteningly human.
Sometimes we are more afraid of being exposed than we are grieved over being false.
More afraid somebody will discover the secret than we are concerned that God already sees it.
More concerned about consequences than repentance.
More concerned about protecting the image than healing the heart.
And perhaps that is why this ancient scene can feel so painfully modern.
Rebekah’s goatskins were practical camouflage.
Genesis does not leave us guessing about the immediate purpose.

Rebekah takes Esau’s best garments and puts them on Jacob. Then she places the goatskins over his hands and the smooth area of his neck. Jacob enters Isaac’s presence carrying the food Rebekah prepared.
Isaac becomes suspicious almost immediately.
“The voice is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau.” — Genesis 27:22
Read that again.
The voice said Jacob.
The hands said Esau.
Something was wrong.
Isaac could hear one identity while touching another.
So he reached out.
And the disguise worked.

The goatskins were there because Rebekah anticipated the possibility that Isaac would test Jacob by touch. Isaac’s eyesight was failing, so the deception had to survive his remaining senses. Esau’s clothing supplied the familiar smell. The prepared meal imitated what Isaac expected from Esau. The goatskins imitated Esau’s hairiness.
This was not a spontaneous little lie.
It became an elaborate impersonation.
And that is where the story becomes more uncomfortable than a Sunday-school retelling sometimes allows.
Jacob was not merely telling a lie.
He was wearing one.
He was standing before his father covered in a manufactured identity.
And some of us know exactly what that feels like.
Not because we have ever wrapped goatskins around our hands.
But because we know what it is to wear something.
The church smile.
The “I’m blessed” response.
The Bible verse posted publicly while privately drowning.
The marriage everyone thinks is fine.
The secret addiction nobody knows about.
The resentment hidden beneath worship songs.
The pornography deleted before anyone checks the phone.
The jealousy disguised as discernment.
The pride disguised as spiritual maturity.
The exhaustion disguised as strength.
The doubt we are terrified to admit.
The sin we keep renaming because calling it what God calls it would require repentance.
Different century.
Different disguise.
Same terrifying instinct.
“Please don’t touch the place where you might discover who I really am.”
But there is another layer to Genesis 27 that must be handled carefully, because it is easy to turn this story into something Scripture itself never says.
God had already spoken concerning Jacob.
Before Jacob and Esau were born, before either brother had performed the events recorded in Genesis 27, the LORD told Rebekah:
“Two nations are in your womb… and the older shall serve the younger.” — Genesis 25:23
God’s sovereign purpose did not originate with Rebekah’s scheme.
That is crucial.
Rebekah did not need to manipulate God into choosing Jacob.
Jacob did not need to deceive Isaac to make God remember His word.
Human beings were trying to secure through manipulation what ultimately depended upon the purposes of God.
That does not make their deception righteous.
It makes the story even more sobering.
Because sometimes our greatest mistakes happen when we believe God’s promise but refuse to trust God’s way.
We pray…
then manipulate.
We say we trust God…
then control everyone around us.
We believe He has a plan…
but panic because His timetable frightens us.
We want the blessing so desperately that we begin justifying whatever appears necessary to obtain it.
And when fear joins faith, we can start doing sinful things while convincing ourselves we are protecting a holy outcome.
God does not need our deception to accomplish His purposes.
He does not need your compromise.
He does not need your manipulation.
He does not need you to become somebody else.
That is one of the great tensions running through Jacob’s life.
Jacob spends much of his early story grasping.
Even his name becomes associated in the narrative with the complicated history of grasping and supplanting.
He wants blessing.
He wants security.
He wants a future.
And in Genesis 27 he walks into his father’s presence dressed like another man to obtain what he desperately desires.
But God is not finished with Jacob.
That may be the most beautiful truth in this entire scandal.
Jacob’s sin has consequences.
This story does not end with Jacob stealing a blessing and riding happily into the sunset.
The family fractures.
Esau is devastated.
Esau plans to kill Jacob.
Jacob flees.
Rebekah sends away the son she was trying so desperately to advance.
Jacob eventually enters the household of Laban, where the deceiver discovers what it feels like to be deceived.
The man who used disguise inside his father’s tent enters years of painful formation.
Sin can be forgiven, but that does not mean sin is harmless.
Grace is not God pretending the wreckage never happened.
Grace is God refusing to let the wreckage have the final word.
And this is where Jacob’s story becomes breathtaking.
Because eventually God meets the deceiver.
Not the costume.
Not Esau’s clothes.
Not the goatskins.
Jacob.
Years later, in Genesis 32, Jacob wrestles through the night and receives a new name.
Israel.
The man who once entered his father’s presence pretending to be somebody else eventually encounters God with nowhere left to hide.
There is something profoundly Gospel-shaped about that movement, even while we must be careful not to claim that every object in Genesis 27 is a direct prophecy.
Genesis never explicitly says, “The goatskins represent Jesus.”
We should not pretend it does.
But the larger biblical story gives Christians something infinitely greater to behold.
Jacob tried to obtain blessing through disguise.
The Gospel announces that sinners are received by God through Christ.
Not because we successfully fool the Father.
Not because we learn to imitate somebody righteous.
Not because we hide our sinful condition well enough.
The exact opposite.
We come into the light.
We confess.
We repent.
We stop pretending.
And we discover that Jesus Christ has done what no disguise could ever accomplish.
“For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.” — 2 Corinthians 5:21
That is not camouflage.
That is redemption.
The New Testament speaks of believers being “in Christ.” Paul can even speak of having “put on Christ” in Galatians 3:27.
But do not miss the difference.
Jacob put on Esau’s clothing in order to deceive his father about who was standing before him.
We are united to Christ not to deceive God, but because God Himself graciously saves sinners through His Son.
God knows exactly who you are.
That is what makes grace astonishing.
He knows.
He knows what happened.
He knows what you watched.
He knows what you said.
He knows what you deleted.
He knows why you did it.
He knows the bitterness.
He knows the envy.
He knows the secret habit.
He knows the nights when your faith felt almost dead.
He knows how much of your public Christianity has sometimes been stronger than your private obedience.
He knows the version of you nobody follows online.
And still the Gospel calls you out of hiding.
Not so that Christ can humiliate the repentant sinner.
So that Christ can save.
That is the scandal of grace.
We spend years stitching together goatskins, while Jesus keeps calling us to come uncovered.
We polish appearances.
Jesus searches hearts.
We manage reputations.
Jesus offers resurrection.
We hide sin.
Jesus shed His blood for sinners.
We attempt to manufacture blessing.
Jesus became the source of eternal salvation for those who belong to Him.
We keep asking, “How can I make myself acceptable?”
And the cross answers, “You cannot save yourself. Come to Christ.”
Maybe that is why this story hurts.
Because eventually every goatskin becomes exhausting to wear.
Pretending is exhausting.
Hiding is exhausting.
Trying to convince everybody you are spiritually healthy while starving inside is exhausting.
Maintaining the reputation of a strong Christian while secretly wondering whether you are becoming cold toward God is exhausting.
And Jesus did not die so you could become better at pretending.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He offers forgiveness.
He transforms people from the inside out.
Maybe your prayer tonight does not need impressive theology.
Maybe it needs honesty.
“Jesus, I’m tired of hiding.”
Maybe repentance begins when your hands stop pretending to belong to somebody else.
Maybe somebody reading this has spent years believing, “If people knew the real me, they would never look at me the same way.”
Perhaps they would not.
But Jesus already knows the real you.
The Gospel does not say your sin is insignificant.
The cross proves sin is deadly serious.
But the cross also proves something else.
God’s mercy is greater than the identity you manufactured to survive without Him.
Christ did not come for imaginary righteous people.
He came to save sinners.
That means you can stop negotiating with the truth.
You can confess.
You can repent.
You can ask forgiveness.
You can make things right where possible.
You can seek accountability.
You can bring hidden darkness into godly light.
And you can trust Jesus rather than the costume.
Someone reading beneath you may need to know they are not the only person fighting to come back into the light.
And please do not keep this article trapped on this page.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It is not.
We glorify God through faith in Christ and lives increasingly surrendered to Him.

But if this ministry is helping you grow in Scripture, confront sin, understand grace, and point people toward Jesus, then supporting and sharing Gospel-centered work can become one practical way of helping truth travel farther.
They look fine.
They post normally.
They laugh.
They work.
They attend church.
And nobody knows how desperately tired they are of pretending.
God does not need the person you pretend to be.
He is calling the person you actually are to Jesus.
But the greatest reason to support Gospel work should never be merchandise.
It should be mission.
Not to prove your faith.
Not to purchase God’s blessing.
Not because clicking “share” makes anyone more righteous.
There may be a Rebekah trying to control what she should have entrusted to God.
There may be an Esau carrying wounds nobody has allowed him to talk about.
There may be someone who believes their scandal disqualified them forever.
Send this story into their darkness.
Because Genesis 27 is not merely a strange ancient story about a mother, two brothers, a blind father, a stolen blessing, and goat skins.
It is a mirror.
It asks what we are wearing.
It asks what we are hiding.
It asks whether we trust God enough to obey Him without manipulating the outcome.
And ultimately, the larger story of Scripture leads us beyond Jacob, beyond Isaac, beyond Esau, beyond Rebekah, beyond every human failure and every human disguise…
to Jesus Christ.
The One who does not need to be deceived into blessing sinners.
The One who already knows the worst chapter.
The One who calls us to repentance rather than performance.
The One whose blood actually cleanses.
The One whose grace does not excuse sin but breaks its dominion.
The One who takes people with scandalous histories and begins writing stories of redemption.
So take off the goatskins.
Come into the light.
Tell Jesus the truth He already knows.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive grace.
And let Christ begin transforming the person you kept trying to hide.
Because one day you may discover that the part of your story you were most desperate to conceal became the very place where people could most clearly see the mercy of Jesus.
You do not have to die wearing the disguise you once believed you needed to survive.
